text:
Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is generally fine on a flight, as long as it goes in your carry-on and not your checked bag.

**The math**
The FAA limit is 100 Wh per power bank. To convert, divide mAh by 1000 and multiply by the voltage. Most power banks use 3.6-3.7 V cells, so:

- 20 Ah × 3.7 V ≈ **74 Wh**, which is under the 100 Wh limit.

Check the label on your unit, since the Wh rating is often printed on it. If it says 20,000 mAh at 3.7 V (or close), you're fine. Some banks list capacity at a higher output voltage (5 V, for example), so use the rated cell capacity or printed Wh if you can.

**Rules to follow**
- **Carry-on only.** Spare lithium batteries and power banks are not allowed in checked baggage. If your carry-on gets gate-checked, take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin. ([FAA: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7))
- **Protect the terminals.** Keep it in its retail packaging, a pouch, or a case, or tape over exposed ports/terminals so nothing can short-circuit it.
- **Don't fly with a damaged or recalled unit.** Swollen, damaged, or recalled batteries aren't allowed.
- **Tell the crew immediately** if it gets hot, swells, smokes, or burns during the flight.
- **Check your airline.** The FAA notes that many airlines have stricter limits, including how many power banks you can bring regardless of capacity. Some airlines also restrict using or charging power banks in flight. Confirm with your carrier before you travel. ([FAA: Airline Passengers and Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries))

**International flights**
IATA's guidance is consistent: keep power banks in hand baggage, protect them from short circuits, and check with your airline, since rules vary by country. ([IATA: Safe Travel with Lithium Batteries](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/))
